newsitem.title: USA: U.S. businessman tangles Mideast peace moves.
newsitem.headline: U.S. businessman tangles Mideast peace moves.

text.p: Israel said on Sunday now was not the time to build another Jewish enclave in Arab East Jerusalem but the U.S. Jewish businessman behind the project dismissed dangers to Middle East peacemaking.
Israel's Jerusalem municipality said on Sunday night two left-wing council members filed an appeal against the project.
One of them, Ornan Yekutieli of Meretz, said he believed the move blocked building of the enclave until a hearing by the Jerusalem District Appeal Committee.

"That's what I understand. Our lawyer is trying to find out. I'll know more tomorrow," Yekutieli told Reuters. Israel Television earlier said a hearing would be held on Monday but Yekutieli said he had yet to be informed of a hearing date.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan said he doubted the appeal would succeed and that it "only postpones the problem, it doesn't solve it".
Bar-Illan said Netanyahu might still have to act against the project, perhaps by invoking public safety or national security.

Irving Moskowitz, a Miami-based Jewish businessman who bankrolls settlement in occupied areas, was granted on Thursday a Jerusalem municipality permit to build some 70 Jewish homes in the 11,000-strong Arab neighbourhood of Ras al-Amoud.

Moskowitz told Israel's army radio on Sunday: "This is not a political issue. It's a simple issue of the right of a property owner to build on his property. To deny it because I am Jewish and Arabs are opposed to it is racism."

He declined comment when asked whether he would heed an appeal from Netanyahu to delay the plan: "The entire subject of whether I should build or not is ludicrous because I have a right to build. It's a democratic country," he said.
Netanyahu was apparently taken by surprise by the project -- which Arab leaders said could wreck peacemaking -- and said he was working to block the plan "at this time".

Relations between Israel and the Palestinians were already in crisis over Israel's breaking ground in March on the Har Homa Jewish settlement on a hilltop, known to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim, on the edge of East Jerusalem.
A senior PLO official said Palestinians didn't believe Netanyahu truly opposed the Ras al-Amoud plan.
"He is trying to improve his image worldwide and give the Americans an excuse to continue pressing the Palestinians to accept Jabal Abu Ghneim," the official told Reuters.
Netanyahu said that Israel would build where it pleased in Jerusalem but the Ras al-Amoud plan's timing was problematic.
"No one should have the false impression that we have changed our policy," a cabinet statement quoted Netanyahu as telling his government after its weekly meeting on Sunday.
Israel occupied Arab East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and says it will never give up an inch of the city.
Palestinians want East Jerusalem as capital of a future state and say building for Jews there pre-empts final peace talks that have yet to begin in earnest.
"You can't allow this provocative project to...further bury the peace process and spark bloodshed," Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's adviser Ahmad Tibi told the radio.
But Moskowitz said: "I expect...if there is any rioting that the government will prevent it."

On Sunday, Western diplomats said the United States was considering a formula to break the peace talks deadlock in which Israel would agree to refrain from building new settlements but could expand existing ones.
Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo said any initiative must include a freeze on settlement building, either permanently or for the length of negotiations.

Palestinian negotiator Nabil Shaath's office on Sunday told Reuters he would meet Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Monday. Israeli officials were not available to comment. A meeting between the two had been agreed on in principle during talks last week between Levy and Arafat in Brussels.
